## 8. Insect Management

### 8.1 Asparagus Beetle, Crioceris asparagi, and Spotted Asparagus Beetle, C. duodecimpunctata

**Time for concern**: Spring through summer.

**Key characteristics:** Common asparagus beetles are 5/16 inch long and black with a blue head, four large yellow spots, and a reddish margin on their abdomen. Spotted asparagus beetles are the same size, but are bright orange with black spots. Adults of both species chew on the spears. Larvae of both species are cream-colored with dark heads and feed for 10 to 14 days. Common asparagus beetles feed on the ferns, whereas spotted asparagus beetles only feed on the fruit on the ferns. Marketable yield can be reduced by feeding damage and the presence of eggs on spears. Feeding on ferns later in the season can reduce plant vigor. See Journal of Integrated Pest Management article [The Common Asparagus Beetle and Spotted Asparagus Beetle](https://academic.oup.com/jipm/article/5/3/B1/2194056) [(Coleoptera: Chrysomelidae): Identification, Ecology, and Management.](https://academic.oup.com/jipm/article/5/3/B1/2194056)

Afternoons are the best time to scout, because that is when adult beetles are most active. Check 20 plants at each of 5 randomly chosen locations in the field and record the numbers of eggs, larvae, and adults. During harvest, consider treatment if more than 2 percent of spears have eggs or if more than 5 percent of spears are infested with asparagus beetle adults. ## 8.2 Asparagus Miner, Ophiomya simplex

**Time of concern:** May through September.

**Key characteristics**: Adult flies are shiny, black, and small (about 1/8 inch to 1/5 inch long). There are two generations per year, with the second generation overwintering as pupae in asparagus stems. Adults from the overwintering generation emerge in May, and mated females deposit eggs beneath the outer layer (epidermis) of the asparagus stem near ground level. Larvae feed on mines within the stem, then pupate in their feeding mines. The second generation of adults emerges in late July and August, and their offspring eventually develop into overwintering pupae. Asparagus miner feeding rarely causes significant yield reductions, and cosmetic damage is usually minimal because mines do not often extend more than a couple of inches above the soil line. The greatest threat from this insect is due to its suspected role in moving Fusarium into asparagus stems. Larval stem tunneling is associated with increased infection with Fusarium, which can significantly reduce the number of years that an asparagus bed remains economically productive. For photos and more information, see Michigan State University [Asparagus Miner Facts](https://www.canr.msu.edu/resources/asparagus_miner_facts_e3143) and Ontario Crop IPM [Asparagus Miner](https://cropipm.omafra.gov.on.ca/en-ca/crops/asparagus/insects-and-mites/20ddcf25-e213-465f-ac1f-181e3db47fe5) fact sheet.
